name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,758

clue.text: Not on a slippery surface in one's workplace?

blocks.note: off is the opposite of on
ice is the classic slippery surface

explanation.surface: Someone worries about slipping over on a freshly mopped or icy floor at work.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the surface is a playful build-up to the place where people work.
explanation.definitionFit: An office is the room or building where a person does their daily job.

clue.text: Trump not in form

blocks.note: out is the opposite of in
a form is a school class

explanation.surface: A comment that a certain politician is having an off day.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T makes 'Trump' look like the politician; here it is the verb meaning to beat. In British schools a form is a class or year group.
explanation.definitionFit: To trump someone is to beat or surpass them, exactly what outclassing a rival means.

clue.text: Amusing to try: I would like a mushroom

blocks.note: to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: Someone at a menu declares they'd fancy trying a mushroom, just for amusement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I would like' reads as a wish, but 'like' belongs to the definition, and 'I would' shrinks to I'D.
explanation.definitionFit: Fungoid is an adjective describing things resembling fungi, of which mushrooms are the familiar example.

clue.text: Medical tube (middle omitted) - put in a member as a plant

indicators.note: the centre letter of the word is left out, so its midpoint is dropped
whatever is put in something ends up inside it, enclosed by the rest

blocks.note: a cannula is a thin tube inserted into the body

explanation.surface: Instructions for a medical procedure, oddly turned into something about a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The tube has seven letters, so its middle is the fourth, an N; the member here is a Member of Parliament, and the inserted pair goes in after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Campanula is the botanical genus of bellflowers, common garden plants with bell-shaped blooms.

clue.text: V&A visitor becoming most faint

blocks.note: the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, letters taken as printed

explanation.surface: A museum-goer at the V&A starts to feel woozy.
explanation.walkthrough: The V&A is the Victoria and Albert Museum in London; its initials supply VA.
explanation.definitionFit: Vague means indistinct or unclear, so the superlative is the least distinct, the faintest.

clue.text: Truly a live rat I slaughtered? Just an experience via a headset!

indicators.note: something slaughtered is cut to pieces, so the letters are chopped up and rearranged

blocks.note: the fourteen letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A rat seems genuinely killed, but it was only a simulation seen through goggles.
explanation.walkthrough: The rat looks real, and the punchline is that it is not; the slaughter is merely the scrambling of the first five words.
explanation.definitionFit: Virtual reality is a computer-simulated world, usually entered by wearing a headset with screens.

clue.text: Mocked great, upstanding newspaper person

indicators.note: in a down entry, standing up means reading from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A fine, honest journalist was ridiculed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upstanding' looks like praise for the journalist's honesty, but it turns the word for great upwards in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: To gibe is to jeer or taunt, so gibed is the past tense of making fun of someone.

clue.text: Daughter standing by river in finale? (To be continued ...)

blocks.note: the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A daughter waits by a river in the last episode of a serial, with the story to be continued.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ure is a Yorkshire river; the loose grammar means the daughter simply comes after it and the finale comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Endured and continued both mean lasted or carried on through time.

clue.text: Sentimentally pretty daughter, initially youthful, resembling a hearty outdoor type

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word it qualifies

blocks.note: twee means excessively cute or quaint
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A sweet young daughter turns out to look like a ruddy country walker.
explanation.walkthrough: Twee is a British word for affectedly quaint or cutesy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweedy describes the countryside set in tweed jackets, a brisk, outdoorsy, rather hearty kind of person.

clue.text: Regain consciousness with feelings of anxiety? Lots of liquids will have this effect

definitions.text: Lots of liquids will have this effect

blocks.note: to surface is to come round or wake up

explanation.surface: Coming round anxious after too many drinks, with a warning about liquids.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots of liquids' reads as heavy drinking, but it means liquids in physics.
explanation.definitionFit: Surface tension is the property of liquids whose molecules pull together at the surface, forming a skin-like film.

clue.text: Bird - stuffed - in cantina, mounted

indicators.note: something stuffed in is packed inside other words, so the answer lies within the letters that follow

blocks.note: runs across the two words, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: A stuffed bird is mounted on the wall of a Mexican bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffed' and 'mounted' read as taxidermy, but the answer simply sits inside the letters of the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The tinamou is a ground-dwelling South and Central American bird related to the ostrich family.

clue.text: Change logo that's about tailless mammal

indicators.note: without a tail means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: a badger is a burrowing mammal

explanation.surface: A company redesigns its emblem around an animal with no tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a preposition in the surface, but it is the short word meaning concerning, as in business letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebadge a product is to relaunch it under a different brand name or emblem.

clue.text: A comic put back: it's available in the bathroom

indicators.note: putting something back sends it in the opposite direction, right to left

blocks.note: a fool is a clown or jester

explanation.surface: A comic book gets returned to its spot beside the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comic' suggests reading matter in the loo; here it is a person, a clown.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofa is the dried fibrous pod of a gourd, used as a bath sponge for scrubbing skin.

clue.text: Discovered deer in trouble as mount went lame

indicators.note: something in trouble is in disorder, so its letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A hunter's horse goes lame just as a troubled deer is spotted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As mount' tells you the lameness is a horse's: foundering is the word for a horse going lame.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse that founders suffers laminitis or collapses, becoming unable to walk properly.

clue.text: I dose child with rum mixture containing zero salt

indicators.note: a mixture blends its ingredients together, so the letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: An irresponsible carer spikes a child's medicine with rum and salt.
explanation.walkthrough: The O for zero joins the letters of the first four words before everything is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Sodium chloride is the chemical name for common table salt.

clue.text: Capek's play has one named woman in imaginary location

blocks.note: R.U.R. is Karel Capek's 1920 robot play

explanation.surface: A Czech playwright's drama features a single named female character in a made-up setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Capek's play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots) gave the world the word robot; its initials start the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruritania is the fictional central European kingdom from Anthony Hope's novel The Prisoner of Zenda.

clue.text: Chaos, taking a very long time to get texts?

explanation.surface: A mobile network failure means texts take forever to arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chaos' reads as the network failure, but it is simply a word for disorder placed before a word for a long stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Texts are short written communications sent by phone, each one a message.

clue.text: Uncontrollable kid? Teen brat joins RN: life changing!

indicators.note: something changing takes on a new form, so these letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: the Royal Navy, letters taken as printed

explanation.surface: A wild teenager is sent into the Royal Navy to be straightened out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the navy will reform the brat; the change is to the letters, not the boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Enfant terrible, French for terrible child, describes a badly behaved child or an unconventional provocateur.

clue.text: Pasta: Italian at last, with a load!

indicators.note: at last points to the closing letter of the word before it

blocks.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: An Italian finally gets a huge plate of pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: Oodles is an informal word for a large quantity, so 'a load' supplies it.
explanation.definitionFit: Noodles are long strips of pasta or similar dough, a staple of many cuisines.

clue.text: This person's so dull, I'm bored stupid!

indicators.note: something stupid is senseless, so these letters make no sense until reordered

blocks.note: letters taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone groans that a companion is so tedious it is numbing their brain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm bored stupid' is a stock phrase; split it into seven letters and the signal to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: A bromide is a tiresome, commonplace person or remark, from the sedative effect of bromide drugs.

clue.text: One's id: that's a particular image

blocks.note: the id, in psychology, is part of one's inner self

explanation.surface: A psychology remark about one's ego and how one sees oneself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's' reads as a connector, but it is the abbreviation i.e., id est, that is.
explanation.definitionFit: A selfie is a photograph a person takes of themselves, a specific kind of picture.

clue.text: Sentimental English movement has rally regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A tearful English protest movement holds a rally.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of the five-letter word are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone moved by or appealing to tender feelings.

clue.text: A particular turn of phrase: "I had" - on the Isle of Man

blocks.note: IOM is the abbreviation for the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A note on a Manx expression, 'I had', used on the island.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man is a self-governing island in the Irish Sea; in a down clue 'on' means placed after.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a set expression whose meaning is peculiar to a language or region.

clue.text: Some reds maybe, as tree initially decays

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word it follows

blocks.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Red autumn leaves appear as a tree begins to decay.
explanation.walkthrough: Reds are left-wingers, not leaves or wines; Trots is informal for Trotskyists.
explanation.definitionFit: Trots, short for Trotskyists, are a kind of communist, hence an example of political reds.

clue.text: He made arty films and collapsed in one

explanation.surface: A film director who made art-house movies and dropped dead in one of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is not a link here; it supplies its own two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Federico Fellini was the Italian director of art-house classics such as La Dolce Vita and 8½.

clue.text: Boy hero getting good, dyeing hair?

blocks.note: Tintin is Hergé's boy reporter hero

explanation.surface: A young hero improves his look with a hair colour.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that tinting is one example of dyeing hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinting is colouring something lightly, as a hairdresser does when giving hair a subtle shade.

clue.text: Former US film producer giving headless animal to chap

indicators.note: without a head means the opening letter is cut off

explanation.surface: A Hollywood mogul hands a decapitated animal to someone, a horse's-head scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film producer' suggests Hollywood; it is film as photographic stock: George Eastman founded Kodak. The beast loses its B.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eastman founded Eastman Kodak, the American company that manufactured roll film for cameras.

clue.text: Has feelings - strongly at first - giving a gentle touch

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word just before it

blocks.note: someone who cares has feelings for others
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone with strong feelings expresses them tenderly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strongly' seems to modify the feelings, but only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A caress is a light, affectionate stroke of the hand, a tender physical gesture.
